correctness.rationale: Direct differentiation verifies H=log(1+alpha x²)/alpha+log(1+beta y²)/beta constant, and grad H vanishes only at origin. Positive levels are regular compact closed ovals and dynamics has no critical points on them. On each quadrant 1+alpha x²=e^(Lu), 1+beta y²=e^(qL(1-u)); the physical-time Jacobian equals (L sqrt(q)/2)e^(-qL/2)e^((q-1)Lu/2)/sqrt((1-e^(-Lu))(1-e^(-qL(1-u)))) and the four symmetric quadrants give period T=2L sqrt(q)e^(-qL/2)Z. For fixed q>1, s=L(1-u) yields q^(-1)B((q-1)/(2q),1/2); for q<1, s=Lu yields B((1-q)/2,1/2). Splitting s at L/2 bounds remote endpoints by decaying exponentials times integrable square-root singularities; it supplies tightness, weak convergence and period coefficients. For q=1+gamma/L, dominated convergence under C[u(1-u)]^(-1/2) proves Z→∫exp(gamma u/2)du and the stated tilted law. All displayed ranges, gamma positive/negative and physical-time normalization were rechecked. Independent sympy differentiation and mpmath 45-digit x-quadrature versus u-quadrature show <=6e-14 relative error in two examples; four fixed-q asymptotic and four crossover numerical specializations agree with the claimed limits. They corroborate but do not prove the infinite limits.
residual_risks: The proof uses elementary dominated convergence rather than formal Lean verification; the numerical tests are finite parameter specializations.
The theorem does not address alpha=0, arbitrary q(L) varying to zero/infinity, or uniform remainders.
